events.excerpt: This discussion is split across two posts because of the forum’s per-post character limit. This first post covers the core interface, growth, authority, and validity. The continuation below covers private presentations, one-time entitlements, recovery, the implementation example, and discussion questions. I am exploring an extension for soulbound credentials that accumulate verified experiences over time and allow those experiences to support different applications. The motivation is: Past activity scattered across different protocols should be reusable as evidence for future eligibility. A person may participate in governance, complete community tasks, provide liquidity, borrow and repay assets, or receive an educational qualification. These experiences can support future requirements such as membership upgrades, contributor access, professional eligibility, or admission to an event. The proposed design uses a persistent, non-transferable credential to maintain continuity across those experiences. Applications can discover its currently accepted state, identify the rules that authorized that state, and evaluate whether the supporting claims remain usable. For privacy-sensitive applications, a holder should be able to prove a requirement such as “I have at least two qualifying contributions and satisfy a balance threshold” without including their complete activity history or exact balance in the presentation. This is a pre-ERC discussion. The core interface and implementation profiles below are proposals for review. No audited implementation or benchmark results are claimed

events.excerpt: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better. Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem. There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd , an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT . Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear. Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands. The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery. Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware."

events.excerpt: This is the discussion thread for EIP-8487 (PR: Add EIP: Separate execution credits and billing credits by Giulio2002 · Pull Request #12637 · ethereum/EIPs · GitHub ). The proposal introduces two counters, both initialized from tx.gasLimit : Credits follow the legacy gas schedule and are the only gas the EVM sees (GAS opcode, call forwarding, creation). Billing follows the new schedule and determines the transaction fee. If billing runs out, the whole transaction aborts (uncatchable), even if credits remain. The goal is to let opcodes be repriced without changing execution behavior for contracts that inspect or forward gas. Open questions: the exact schedules, charge points, rebate rules, receipt fields and block accounting. Feedback welcome. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic
